content: The outcomes of interest in the studies included uncomplicated malaria, severe malaria, and anemia. Additional outcomes assessed were hospital admissions (both all-cause and malaria-specific), all-cause mortality, adverse events, drug-vaccine interactions, parasite prevalence, and the need for blood transfusions. Twelve trials were included in the review, three of which were cluster-randomized controlled trials. All trials were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in Gabon, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Mozambique, Uganda, and the United Republic of Tanzania. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) was evaluated in 10 trials, amodiaquine in one trial, artesunate-amodiaquine (AS-AQ) in one trial, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-P) in one trial, and SP combined with artesunate (SP+AS) in one trial. The systematic review included trials comparing preventive malaria chemoprevention (PMC) with no intervention in young children aged 8 weeks to 24 months, with follow-up periods ranging from 9 to 36 months of age. Most studies administered 3–4 doses of antimalarial drugs. The AMSTAR-2 checklist assessment concluded that the systematic review was well-conducted and addressed most of the outcomes identified by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in the PICO question. The GDG considered that PMC likely increases health equity when delivered through the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) platform, as EPI access is generally equitable and coverage tends to be high. More information on the evidence is available in the summary of contextual factors report. PMC has been widely accepted by caregivers, particularly when delivered alongside vaccinations through the EPI platform. The EPI itself is generally well-accepted and perceived as beneficial. Although some healthcare workers expressed dissatisfaction with the process of administering PMC and noted an increased workload, most had positive perceptions of PMC, with some suggesting it improved EPI attendance. The GDG considered PMC to be probably acceptable to key stakeholders. Despite logistical challenges such as access to clean water, crushing tablets, and occasional drug shortages, PMC implementation appears feasible when delivered through the EPI platform. The GDG deemed PMC implementation to be feasible. More information on the evidence can be found in the summary of contextual factors report. The systematic review did not cover some outcomes of interest to the GDG, such as malaria-specific hospital admissions, blood transfusions, and potential drug-vaccine interactions. The GDG determined that the balance between desirable and undesirable effects favored PMC. Moderate costs were associated with PMC implementation through EPI, and PMC was considered probably cost-effective. However, alternative delivery strategies to EPI or the use of more expensive antimalarials could affect cost-effectiveness. The GDG concluded that a conditional recommendation should be made for PMC based on its moderate beneficial effect and moderate certainty of evidence. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) involves the intermittent administration of a curative dose of antimalarial medicine during the malaria season, regardless of whether the child is infected. The goal of SMC is to establish antimalarial drug concentrations in the blood that clear existing infections and prevent new ones during periods of highest malaria risk. SMC is recommended in areas with seasonal malaria transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using a combination medicine for SMC that differs from the first-line treatment for malaria. The component medicines should have closely matched pharmacology to minimize the risk of new infections encountering only a single drug. SP+AQ has been widely used for SMC in Africa and has been shown to be efficacious, safe, well-tolerated, available, and inexpensive. The prevalence of molecular markers of resistance to SP+AQ was low in the general population before and two years after SMC implementation in seven countries in West and Central Africa. Safety and efficacy have been evaluated for several other drug combinations, but the lack of widescale implementation means fewer data are available on potential risks of cumulative toxicity and the impact on drug resistance. Most research studies have evaluated SMC in children aged 3–59 months. SMC has also been shown to reduce the incidence of clinical malaria in children under 10 years old. Studies in one country comparing the effect of SMC among children under 5 years old with those aged 5–9 years found no difference in effect size for malaria incidence, prevalence, severe malaria, or anemia. The age group targeted for SMC should be informed by the local age pattern of severe malaria admissions. The cost-effectiveness of SMC becomes less favorable as programs expand to age groups at lower risk of severe disease and areas of lower malaria transmission. Children in age groups at increased risk of severe disease should receive a complete course of antimalarials at their recommended treatment dose as SMC. Drug dosage should be determined by the child’s weight whenever possible, with age-based dosing used only when weight is unknown. The number of SMC cycles should be informed by the duration of the high-transmission season, based on local malaria epidemiology and the length of preventive efficacy of the selected drug combination. SMC should protect children during the entire high-transmission season. Current evidence supports monthly administration of SMC for 3–4 cycles in shorter transmission settings, and up to six cycles have been evaluated in settings with longer transmission seasons. SMC can be delivered through door-to-door or fixed-point delivery. Studies in Mali and Gambia have shown that door-to-door delivery can achieve high coverage. Similar SMC coverage was observed in children receiving directly observed treatment compared to non-directly observed treatment. While some prospective trials and ecological studies of SMC with SP+AQ in West Africa have reported increased prevalence of certain resistance mutations, no evidence has been found of SMC leading to higher-level resistance mutations that severely impair SP efficacy. SMC does not appear to select for parasites carrying mutations associated with diminished AQ susceptibility. SMC is not recommended for children with severe acute illness, those unable to take oral medication, children who received a dose of any SMC drugs in the last 30 days, or those with allergies to the drugs used. Children receiving sulfa-based medications, such as co-trimoxazole, should not receive SMC including SP. Information about SMC should be fully accessible to caregivers and key stakeholders, such as government officials and religious leaders. Consent should be obtained from caregivers on behalf of the child before administering SMC. The GDG considered the overall costs of implementing SMC to be moderate. Expanding SMC to children in age groups beyond those at highest risk of severe disease, areas of lower malaria transmission, or using more expensive antimalarials may affect cost-effectiveness.
